opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a straight line. When I started my PhD, I wasn't thinking "attention" as a research topic. I was more interested in the broader question of why large models work as well as they do, and where they break.

What pulled me toward attention was that, as models scaled up, it became clear that so much of their behavior, both the impressive parts and the failures, is mediated by how attention distributes information across tokens. Some of the strange phenomena people kept noticing, like models putting huge attention weight on the first token, or struggling to use information in the middle of a long context, all pointed back to the attention mechanism. These weren't just engineering quirks. They told you something about what the model had actually learned to do.

There was also a very practical side. Attention is the part of the Transformer that scales quadratically with sequence length, so once everyone wanted longer contexts, it became the bottleneck for both efficiency and capability. That made it a place where understanding and engineering meet. If you really understand what the attention heads are doing, you can make principled decisions about what to compress, what to keep, and how to design alternatives.

So it was a mix of curiosity and timing. It felt like the component everyone used but nobody fully understood, and that kind of gap is usually a good place to do research.

r001.rationale: The response says attention drew his interest through model behavior, long-context issues, and efficiency bottlenecks. It does not attribute his focus to extensive experimentation with Value Potential Learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a plan. I started out, like a lot of people in my cohort, working on model architecture more broadly—the question I cared about was efficiency, how to get more out of the same compute. And every time I traced a bottleneck back to its source, I ended up at the same place: the attention layer. Memory, latency, scaling with sequence length—it was always attention sitting at the center.

At some point I stopped treating it as an obstacle in the way of my "real" research and started treating it as the research. What struck me was how much the whole field had converged on one mechanism, almost by accident, without a very deep understanding of why it works as well as it does, or where it breaks. There were a lot of folk beliefs: "the model attends to the important tokens," that kind of thing. When I actually looked at the attention maps, they were much stranger than that—attention sinks, heads that seemed to do nothing, heads that were doing something clever but completely unintuitive.

That mismatch between how central the mechanism is and how poorly it was understood is what pulled me in. There's also a personal reason. I like problems where theory and engineering meet. With attention, you can't separate them: a mathematically elegant variant that doesn't map well onto GPU memory hierarchies is worthless in practice, and a hardware trick that changes the math in ways you don't understand will bite you at scale. So it forces you to think on both levels at once, which I find very satisfying.

And then, frankly, long context became the thing everyone needed. Suddenly the quadratic cost wasn't an academic concern anymore—it was the thing determining what products could exist. So the timing worked out. But I'd say the real origin was just following the bottleneck until I realized the bottleneck was the most interesting part.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his focus to following model-efficiency bottlenecks to the attention layer and studying attention’s behavior. It does not mention extensive experimentation with Value Potential Learning.

astra-6.text: What drew me to attention was a simple question: why do some things occupy our minds while others barely register? We can encounter the same information at different moments and have completely different experiences of it, depending on where our attention is. That made attention seem like a useful starting point for understanding how we learn and make decisions. And the more I thought about it, the more interesting the question became: are we choosing what to pay attention to, or is something else doing the choosing for us?

r001.rationale: The response describes general curiosity about attention, learning, and decision-making, but does not attribute Su Tinghao’s focus to extensive experimentation with Value Potential Learning.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it started with a simple question: why do some things capture our attention while others pass unnoticed? That led me to think about attention as more than concentration. It shapes what we notice, what we learn, and what we remember. The more I thought about those connections, the more attention became the question I wanted to focus on.
